previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 54-year-old woman with a history of Crohn’s disease, short bowel syndrome, and SVC syndrome was admitted with worsening symptoms of superior vena cava obstruction, including neck swelling, headache, blurry vision, and nausea. Imaging confirmed patent internal jugular veins, but a diagnostic SVC-IVC venogram revealed persistent SVC obstruction. An attempted stent placement was unsuccessful, and cardiothoracic surgery was consulted for future bypass planning. A blood culture showed coagulase-negative staph and Enterococcus faecium, but antibiotics were discontinued as the result was deemed a contaminant. Abdominal imaging indicated ileus related to a Crohn’s flare, managed conservatively. The patient improved symptomatically and was discharged home with a plan for outpatient surgical evaluation, medication adjustments, and follow-up.

Brief Hospital Course:
Ms. ___ is an unfortunate woman with long history of Crohns

patch angioplasty.  The procedure was uncomplicated.  PLease see

was also started on IV lopressor for hypertension, which was 
converted to POs once she was tolerating a diet.  She was

subcutaneous tissues.  Thus her left groin line was pulled.  
Chronic pain service was consulted to assist in PO pain 
management, and recommended morphine elixer, which actually 
controlled her pain relatively well.  She was also restarted on 
valium, benadryl, and phenergan PRN.

Her hematocrit continued to trend down slowly, to a low of 21.5 
on POD 5.  She also had some bowel movements that were 
reportedly mixed with blood, and did have guaiac positive 
stools.  Cdif toxin was found to be negative.  As she did not 
have IV access, she was given a dose of subcutaeous Epogen and 
oral lasix.  Her hematocrit was found to be 26.5 at the time of 
discharge.  She was evaluated by physical therapy, who 
determined that she was safe for discharge home.  She will be 
discharged with 6 days worth of her current pain/anxiety 
medications, which are working pretty well for her.  A followup 
appointment has been made with her PCP ___ 4 days to assess her 
need for further pain medications, and check her hematocrit.

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  ___ woman, status post subclavian bypass.  Assess for lines
and/or pneumothorax.

COMPARISON:  Pre-operative chest radiograph on ___.

SINGLE PORTABLE SEMI-UPRIGHT CHEST RADIOGRAPH:  The patient is mildly rotated
to the right.  New clips are noted at the right supraclavicular region.  New
sternotomy wires are intact.  The endotracheal tube terminates approximately
2.0 cm above the carina.  The nasogastric tube is seen traversing through the
stomach.  There are two chest tubes in the medial right apex, and a third in
the medial left lung base.  

The lung volumes are low.  Mildly prominent pulmonary vasculature suggests
mild fluid overload.  There is no pneumothorax or pleural effusion. 
Persistent right apical opacity is more prominent in the current study,
probably rotational artifacts and/or post-surgical.  Small amount of
subcutaneous gas in the right lateral neck is in keeping with recent surgery.

IMPRESSION:
1.  No pneumothorax or pleural effusion.  Endotracheal tube terminates 2.0 cm
above the carina.  Chest tubes as described above.
3.  Right apical opacity more prominent, could be atelectasis, artefactual or
post-surgical.  Recommend repeating chest radiograph with true frontal view to
re-assess.

SINGLE AP PORTABLE VIEW OF THE CHEST

REASON FOR EXAM:  Status post SVC reconstruction, status post chest tube
removal, assess for pneumothorax.

Comparison is made with prior study performed a day earlier.

There is no pneumothorax.  If any, there is a small right pleural effusion. 
Cardiac size is top normal.  Sternal wires are aligned.  Right upper lobe
opacity has improved, consistent with improving atelectasis.  Vascular
congestion has resolved.

AP CHEST 10:15 P.M. ___  

HISTORY:  Brachiocephalic vein repair.  Fever.

IMPRESSION:  AP chest compared to ___:

Right upper paratracheal region of the mediastinum and the apical pleural
margin are both slightly wider today than on ___ at 9:20 a.m.  Whether this
is the expected post-operative appearance would depend upon timing of vascular
reconstruction, not noted in the request.  Therefore some upper mediastinal
bleeding should be considered.  There is also new consolidation in the right
upper lobe marginating the major fissure, could be atelectasis or developing
pneumonia.  Small right pleural effusion is new.  There is no pulmonary edema.
Heart size is normal.  Dr. ___ was paged to report these findings at the
time of dictation.

HISTORY:  ___ woman status post bypass with abdominal distention.

COMPARISON:  Abdominal x-ray from ___.

FINDINGS:  Four images of the abdomen are obtained, two supine and two
lateral.  There is a mild dilation of the small bowel throughout, all less
than 6 cm.  The osseous structures are normal.  There is a catheter projecting
over the left hemipelvis.  Sternal wires are seen.  There is no free air
noted.

IMPRESSION:  Borderline distention of the bowel loops may represent ileus.

INDICATION:  Evaluate L groin line; evaluate for abdominal pain and
distention.

COMPARISON:  CT abdomen on ___.

TECHNIQUE:  5-mm axial sections were taken from the base of the lungs to the
pelvis.  Sagittal and coronal reformats were obtained.  Oral contrast was
given.  120 cc of Optiray IV contrast was pushed by hand through the left
groin line.

FINDINGS:  Limited evaluation of the base of the lungs shows moderate
bilateral effusions with associated atelectasis.  There was no pneumonia or
evidence of interstitial pulmonary edema.  There is a new small-to-moderate
pericardial effusion which is likely hemorrhagic based on Hounsfield units. It
is slightly more dense than simple fluid.  This is likely an expected
postoperative change after sternotomy.  The sternotomy wire borders appear to
be overlapping in the sternum.  There is a small amount of air in the
subcutaneous soft tissue anterior to the sternum.

The liver is unremarkable.  The patient is status post cholecystectomy.  The
spleen, adrenals, kidneys and pancreas all are unremarkable.  The small bowel
is not distended.  The large bowel is also not distended without evidence of
obstruction.  At its largest diameter it measures 5.8 cm with normal being up
to 6 cm.  There is no free air in the abdomen.  No lymphadenopathy is noted.

There is active contrast extravasation into the left perivascular space. There
is a probable hematoma medial to this contrast extravasation.  This is
displacing the urinary bladder slightly to the right.  A Foley catheter is
seen in the bladder.

There are no abnormalities or lesions seen in the bone.  There are multiple
subcutaneous calcifications consistent with injection granulomas.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Contrast accumulation into perivascular space secondary to malposition of
the femoral central line.  An adjacent hematoma is present in the
preperitoneal space.
2.  New pericardial effusion, likely with hemorrhagic component.  These are
probably normal postoperative changes.
3.  Bilateral pleural effusions with associated atelectasis.
4.  No evidence of small bowel obstruction or ileus.
